analysis.headline: S. 1, the For the People Act of 2021, had 48 cosponsors but the Senate Rules Committee failed to report it favorably; it was discharged by a party-line 50-49 vote and placed on the Senate calendar, where it never received an up-or-down vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The For the People Act was an omnibus bill covering voting access, campaign finance, and government ethics. It would have required states to offer automatic and same-day voter registration, at least two weeks of early voting, and no-excuse vote-by-mail; set up independent commissions to draw congressional districts; mandated paper ballots and election-security grants; created a small-donor public financing system for congressional campaigns; required disclosure of big political spending; and imposed new ethics rules, including a Supreme Court code of conduct and ten years of tax return disclosure for presidents and vice presidents.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, especially those who face barriers to registration and in-person voting: people who move frequently, work inflexible hours, have disabilities, live on Indian lands, or were disenfranchised by felony convictions. Small-dollar donors would gain matching public funds that multiply their political voice. Voters in gerrymandered districts would gain from independent redistricting commissions.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require states to automatically register eligible citizens from agency records (unless they decline), offer same-day registration, and provide online registration and updates.
It would mandate early voting, no-excuse voting by mail, ballot tracking, and secured drop boxes, and limit removal of voters from registration rolls.
It would require states to adopt independent redistricting commissions for congressional maps and ban mid-decade redistricting.

It would establish election-security measures, including grants for paper-ballot systems, risk-limiting audits, sharing threat intelligence with state election officials, and a bug bounty program for election systems.
It would create a public financing system with small-donor matching funds for Senate and presidential campaigns, and require disclosure of campaign spending, including online political ads.

It would impose new ethics rules on all three branches, including a code of conduct for Supreme Court justices, conflict-of-interest rules for the executive branch, and ten years of tax return disclosure for the president and vice president.

analysis.who_pays: Large donors, super PACs, and 'dark money' nonprofit spenders would lose the advantages of undisclosed and unlimited political spending through the DISCLOSE Act, Honest Ads, and small-donor public financing provisions [S2][S3]. The lobbying industry would face expanded disclosure and registration requirements [S3]. Incumbent members of Congress and state legislators who currently draw their own district maps would lose that power to independent commissions, potentially making many seats competitive [S2][S3]. Foreign nationals seeking to influence elections would face expanded prohibitions and criminal penalties for undisclosed involvement [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill would preempt state election laws with detailed federal mandates on registration, early voting, and mail voting, raising federalism objections from opponents who argue election administration is a state responsibility.

Automatic registration through agencies including firearms-regulating agencies, colleges, and federal databases would transfer personal data to election officials by default unless individuals opt out, which critics have raised as an accuracy and privacy concern.
The small-donor matching program and election grants would require substantial federal spending, and the bill includes no offsetting revenue.

The bill itself concedes its constitutional footing would be contested: Section 3 contains extensive 'findings of general constitutional authority' defending Congress's power under the Elections Clause and the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments, and Section 4 channels all constitutional challenges to the D.C. courts, anticipating litigation over provisions such as nationwide independent redistricting commissions.

The discharge vote that freed the bill from committee passed 50-49, falling one vote short of a simple majority and far short of the 60 votes needed to end debate in the Senate, meaning even full floor consideration was not achievable under normal rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits to voters were broad but indirect: easier registration and voting, more secure elections, and cleaner financing of campaigns would apply to everyone, but no individual would receive a direct cash benefit. The costs fell on identifiable, powerful groups—big spenders, lobbyists, and incumbents who draw their own maps—which is precisely why opposition concentrated. The main design criticisms are legitimate: it is a one-size-fits-all federal mandate on state-run elections, its automatic registration data flows raise privacy questions, and its public financing is costly. Whether those drawbacks outweigh expanding access to voting depends on how much weight one gives the constitutional tradition of federal protection of the franchise, which the bill itself invokes at length.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Rules and Administration Committee failed to report the bill favorably on May 11, 2021; the Senate then discharged the committee by a party-line 50-49 vote on August 11, 2021, placed the bill on the Legislative Calendar, and never brought it to an up-or-down vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: S. 1 was introduced on March 17, 2021 by Sen. Jeff Merkley with 48 cosponsors (46 Democrats and 2 Independents), and was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration.
The Rules and Administration Committee held hearings on March 24, 2021, printing S.Hrg. 117-14, but on May 11, 2021 the committee failed to report the bill favorably.

On August 11, 2021, the Senate discharged the committee by a yea-nay vote of 50-49 (Record Vote 358, pursuant to S. Res. 27): all 48 Democrats and both Independents voting yea, all 49 Republicans voting nay.

The bill was then placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 123), but the Senate never took it up for floor consideration, and it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

key_actors.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee
key_actors.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-MN)
key_actors.what_they_did: Held hearings on March 24, 2021, then failed to report the bill favorably on May 11, 2021, preventing it from advancing with a committee report.

key_actors.name: 49 Senate Republicans
key_actors.what_they_did: Voted unanimously (49 nay) against the motion to discharge the bill from committee on August 11, 2021, and none supported it at any stage in the record.

key_actors.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
key_actors.what_they_did: Was an original cosponsor and, as majority leader, brought the motion to discharge the committee from the bill under S. Res. 27, which passed 50-49 and placed the bill on the calendar; no floor vote followed.

key_actors.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
key_actors.what_they_did: Introduced S. 1 on March 17, 2021 and recruited 48 cosponsors (46 Democrats, 2 Independents) for the omnibus voting, campaign finance, and ethics bill.
